issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: For a 77-year-old female surgeon whose index trauma is life-threatening illness, avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. It implies a trauma context involving armed threat, which is not represented in the memory or appraisal items and is inconsistent with the formulation, where Triggers are inactive and not linked to other nodes. This item is therefore clinically incoherent with the stated trauma and node pattern.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: For a 77-year-old divorced female surgeon with trauma type of life-threatening illness, this appraisal is not impossible but is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on disrupted autobiographical memory, identity change, loss of faith, rumination/positive reframing, and avoidance of medical cues related to illness. 'Lost community and culture' introduces a social/cultural disconnection theme that is not supported by the other selected items or by the formulation's strong Memory/Maladaptive Strategies/Negative Appraisals loop. It reads as an isolated appraisal rather than one plausibly emerging from the presented illness-related memory and coping pattern. The remaining items are broadly coherent with each other and with the formulation.

vignette: Leilani had always been a woman of precision and control. As a renowned surgeon, she had spent decades honing her skills in the operating room, earning the respect of her peers and the gratitude of her patients. But it was during her own brush with mortality that Leilani's world began to unravel. It started with a diagnosis: stage III ovarian cancer. The news hit Leilani like a ton of bricks, forcing her to confront the possibility of her own death. As she underwent treatment, Leilani found herself preoccupied with the question of why this was happening to her. She would lie awake at night, searching for answers that never seemed to come. "Why me?" she would ask herself, as if repeating a mantra. As the months dragged on, Leilani began to notice gaps in her memory. There were moments from her treatment that she simply couldn't recall, no matter how hard she tried. She remembered the sound of beeping machines and the antiseptic smell of the hospital, but entire conversations with her doctors and loved ones had vanished into thin air. When memories did resurface, they came in fragmented pieces – a disconnected jumble of images and emotions that refused to cohere. Leilani's attempts to make sense of these memories only seemed to drive her further into confusion. She would find herself reliving moments from the hospital with perfect clarity, only to have them fade away like sand between her fingers. Some days, she felt like she was losing her grip on reality itself. The person she had once been – confident, capable, and in control – now seemed like a distant stranger. As Leilani struggled to come to terms with her new reality, she began to avoid medical cues that might trigger memories of her illness. Hospitals, ambulances, and even routine physical examinations became sources of dread. She would force herself to think only positive thoughts when these fears arose, as if willing herself into a state of denial. But the truth was, Leilani had lost faith in everything she once believed in. People, life itself – it all seemed so fragile and capricious now. The identity she had built around her work and her sense of self-worth had been irreparably damaged. She no longer recognized herself in the mirror; the woman staring back was a stranger, worn down by fear and uncertainty. Leilani's relationships began to suffer as well. Colleagues who had once admired her precision and skill now saw a shadow of her former self – distant, detached, and increasingly isolated. Her children and grandchildren tried to reach out, but Leilani pushed them away, unsure of how to articulate the turmoil brewing inside. It was only when she found herself unable to perform even routine surgeries that Leilani realized she needed help. The tremors in her hands were now matched by a crippling sense of anxiety – the fear that she would one day forget something crucial, or worse, lose control entirely. As she sat in her office, staring blankly at the medical diplomas on her wall, Leilani knew it was time to confront the darkness head-on. She picked up the phone and dialed a therapist's number, hoping against hope that someone could help her find her way back – not just as a surgeon, but as herself.
